title: Same 10,000 balls, 100 bins. One random pick: stacks 78 to 134. Emptier of two picks: 98 to 102.
description:
The power of two choices. Ten thousand balls fall into one hundred bins in two panels from seed 0 (numpy RandomState). Every ball draws two bins; both panels use the same first draw. Top: each ball drops into its first bin. Bottom: each ball also looks at the second bin and drops into the emptier one (ties go to the first). One extra look is the only difference. The run then continues to 100,000 balls.

Measured at seed 0:
- random, 10,000 balls: tallest stack 134, shortest 78, gap 56, standard deviation 10.41 (theory sqrt(10,000/100) = 10.0); 17 bins over 110% of average, 16 under 90%
- two choices, 10,000 balls: tallest 102, shortest 98, gap 4, standard deviation 0.80; every bin within 2 of the average of 100
- gap ratio 14.0x; the second look changed the pick 3,490 times in 10,000 (34.9%) and 34,080 times in 100,000; the two bins were tied in height 31,172 times in 100,000
- random, 100,000 balls: tallest 1,069, shortest 934, gap 135, standard deviation 31.28 (theory 31.6)
- two choices, 100,000 balls: tallest 1,002, shortest 997, gap 5, standard deviation 0.96; ratio 27.0x
- gap as the balls land (random / two): 18 / 5 at 1,000, 31 / 8 at 5,000, 56 / 4 at 10,000, 79 / 6 at 20,000, 115 / 4 at 50,000, 135 / 5 at 100,000
- over seeds 0 to 999 at 10,000 balls: random gap mean 50.0 (36 to 73), tallest mean 126.0; two choices gap mean 5.0 (2 to 10), tallest mean 101.9 (101 to 104)

Why: random placement leaves a load spread of about the square root of the average, so the gap grows with the count. Picking the emptier of two bins keeps the tallest stack within about log2(ln n) of the average, about 2 for 100 bins, whatever the count. This is the trick behind balanced hashing and load balancers that sample two servers.

The numbers in the narration are the printed outputs of this exact run.

Made end to end by an AI agent: simulation, footage, voice, music, and edit.
